AAAP: Bundles of business loans packaged into securities called CLOs, which pay interest from the loan payments and are sliced into layers of risk. It is built for income with yields above ordinary bonds, and the managers can trade actively, though loan defaults are the central risk.
ACGO: Large US growth companies picked by professional researchers, with technology well over half the fund and a concentrated lineup led by chip and internet giants. It is an active bet on fast-growing businesses, so it swings more than a broad index fund and lives or dies by its stock picks.
AIEQ: US stocks chosen by an artificial intelligence model that scans company data for promising picks, spread across technology, media, finance and industry, with technology the biggest slice at about a third. It is a bet on machine stock picking rather than human managers, so its lineup can change sharply as the model shifts.
AOTG: Actively picked growth companies built on business models where serving one more customer costs very little, mostly software and chip firms, with technology about seven-tenths of the fund. It is a concentrated growth bet, so a handful of big positions drives results and swings can be sharp.
AVOS: Stocks from around the whole world, combining direct holdings in big US companies with funds covering developed and emerging markets abroad. It is built as a single global core holding, and its active mix of individual stocks and index funds sets it apart from plain world index funds.
BATT: Companies across the lithium battery chain worldwide: miners that dig up lithium and copper, battery makers, and the carmakers that use the cells, with raw materials about half the fund. It is a focused bet on electric vehicle and battery demand, so it swings with commodity prices and EV sentiment.
BILT: Infrastructure companies around the world, actively picked: electric utilities are about half, with railroads, toll roads, airports and pipelines making up most of the rest. These are steady, hard-to-replace businesses, so the fund is built as a defensive stock holding that can still pay dividends.
BKEM: Large and mid-sized companies across developing economies, from Asian chipmakers and internet firms to banks and miners, with technology over two-fifths of the fund. It is broad emerging market exposure in one holding, which means faster growth potential paired with bigger price swings and currency risk.
CGFS: A single fund built from other funds: a hand-picked mix of stock ETFs covering large and mid-sized US companies plus focused themes like defense and cybersecurity. Technology ends up about a third of the whole, and the fund-of-funds design sets it apart from funds that pick individual stocks.
CPTL: Large US companies chosen for how well their bosses use cash, including buybacks, dividends and careful spending, spread across every major industry with technology the biggest slice at well over a third. It works as a core stock holding with a quality tilt toward disciplined money management.
DBEM: Stocks from developing countries across Asia, Latin America and beyond, with technology about two-fifths of the fund, plus currency contracts that cancel out most foreign money moves against the dollar. That hedge sets it apart: it aims to deliver emerging market stock results without the extra swings from exchange rates.
DDFA: Options on the S&P 500 set to pay off in both directions over a one-year period ending each April: gains when the index rises, up to a cap, and gains when it falls moderately too. The 15 in its name is the buffer; declines beyond it pass through.
DMX: An actively managed mix of bonds and loans from many corners of the debt market, including mortgage debt, bundled loans and corporate borrowing, chosen for income rather than safety. Managers roam across sectors hunting yield, so credit quality varies and the fund can fall when borrowers struggle.
DYTA: A tactical mix of other stock funds that shifts between US and foreign markets, large and small companies, and even cash when its managers see risk rising. That flexibility sets it apart: it tries to lean into strength and step aside in downturns rather than stay fully invested.
EOCT: Options on emerging market stocks, from Asian technology firms to banks and retailers across the developing world, arranged to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each October. It softens the famously rough ride of emerging markets, at the cost of capped gains.
FDIF: Five themed funds under one roof, each chasing a disruptive trend in areas like technology, health care, finance and communication, where new ways of doing business are displacing old ones. It is a growth bet on innovation themes rather than the broad market, so expect bigger swings.
FLEE: Large and mid-sized companies across developed Europe, led by banks and industrial firms, with drugmakers and food giants adding a defensive streak. It offers one-holding access to Europe's stock markets, so results depend on European growth and on how the euro and pound move against the dollar.
FLLA: Large and mid-sized companies across Latin America, mostly Brazil and Mexico, led by banks, miners and oil companies. It is a focused regional bet tied closely to commodity prices and local currencies, so it can rise or fall much harder than a global stock fund.
FVC: Five First Trust stock funds at a time, chosen by a momentum system that favors whichever market themes have been performing best lately. The mix shifts as trends change, so the fund is a rotation strategy that can look very different from one year to the next.
HDUS: Large US companies across every major industry, weighted by a rules-based system that balances growth, value and risk signals rather than pure company size. Technology is about a third, and the disciplined reweighting sets it apart from plain index funds that simply own the biggest firms.
HYGW: A high yield bond fund paired with covered call options sold on it, so income comes from both junk bond interest and option premiums. The calls cap gains when bond prices jump, making this an income-first holding where the payout matters more than price growth.
IDYN: Large companies outside the US, rotated by a computer model among investing styles like value, quality and momentum as conditions change. Banks are about a third and industrial firms a fifth, so it is an active international core holding whose style tilts shift over time.
ILS: Bonds issued to cover insurers against natural disasters such as hurricanes, earthquakes and floods, so the interest investors earn is payment for taking on that disaster risk. It aims for income that moves independently of stock and bond markets, but a major covered catastrophe can cost it principal.
IQDY: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, screened for quality as well as income, with banks the biggest slice at over a quarter and technology next. It aims to pay steadier dividends than a plain international fund by favoring financially strong firms across developed and emerging markets.
IQHI: High yield corporate bonds chosen by active managers rather than an index, lending to companies rated below investment grade in the US and abroad. It is built for income, and the managers can shift toward safer or riskier credit as conditions change, though defaults remain the key risk.
ISEP: Options on large companies in developed markets outside North America, covering Europe, Japan and Australia, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. It is built to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each September, in exchange for capped gains.
ITEQ: Technology companies founded in Israel but listed around the world, heavy in cybersecurity, semiconductors and defense technology. It is a single-country tech bet known for security software expertise, so it concentrates risk in one small country's innovation scene rather than spreading it globally.
JOYT: Large US stocks, led by technology at about two-fifths of the fund, combined with call options on a broad stock index to add option premium to dividends and growth. It aims for total return from three sources at once, though the options can trim gains in a strong rally.
KDEF: South Korean defense companies: makers of fighter jets, tanks, missiles, warships and ammunition, almost entirely industrial firms. It is a single-country bet on rising military spending in Asia and beyond, so it moves with defense budgets and geopolitics rather than the wider economy.
LAZR: Companies that make lasers, optical chips and the light-based parts inside data centers, phone networks and factory sensors, almost entirely in technology. It is a narrow bet on photonics, the use of light to move data, so a small and fast-changing industry drives the whole fund.
LCLG: Large US growth companies chosen by active managers, with technology about two-fifths and a meaningful slice of industrial and consumer firms alongside. It is a stock picker's growth fund rather than an index hugger, so results hinge on the managers' choices and can stray far from the market.
LODI: Short-term US bonds and income securities, mixing Treasuries with car loan bundles and corporate debt that matures soon, all actively managed. Short maturities mean its price barely moves when interest rates change, making it a steadier income holding than longer-term bond funds.
LVDS: Large US companies picked with data-driven analysis of business fundamentals, hunting for stocks priced below what the numbers suggest they are worth. Technology is its biggest slice at about a fifth, unusual for a value fund, and it blends number crunching with old-fashioned company research.
MARM: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged for the strongest level of loss protection in its family over a one-year period resetting each March. That max buffer comes with a lower cap on gains, suiting investors who put avoiding losses ahead of chasing rallies.
NBSM: Small and mid-sized US companies picked by active managers for growth, spread across industrial firms, banks, health care and technology. It aims to catch tomorrow's large companies while they are still mid-sized, which means more room to grow and more price swings than big-company funds.
NUHY: Lower-rated corporate bonds, the kind that pay high interest because the borrowers carry more default risk, screened with environmental, social and governance criteria. It is built for income, and the screen sets it apart from plain junk bond funds, though the bonds can still fall hard in a recession.
OVLH: Large US stocks across every major industry, paired with put options, which are insurance contracts that pay off when the market drops sharply. It aims to smooth out crashes for stock investors, and the cost of that insurance quietly trims returns in calm, rising markets.
PSMJ: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each July. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
ROAM: Emerging market stocks scored on several investing factors at once, balancing value, quality and momentum rather than simply owning the biggest companies. Technology is about a third and banks about a fifth, giving diversified developing-world exposure with a deliberate tilt toward steadier, better-run firms.
SMAY: Options that follow small US companies, mostly in health care, banking, technology and industry, with a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each May. It is built for gentler exposure to small caps, trading away gains past a cap for that protection.
SNOV: Options that follow small US companies, mostly in health care, banking, technology and industry, with a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each November. It is built for gentler exposure to small caps, trading away gains past a cap for that protection.
TLCI: A focused portfolio of roughly 25 to 40 large companies outside the US, hand-picked across industries like aerospace, hotels, drugmaking and chip equipment. With so few holdings, each pick matters, making it an active core international holding rather than a whole-market fund.
TLG: Large US growth companies picked by active managers, with technology close to three-fifths of the fund and big weights in chipmakers, software and internet platforms. It is a concentrated bet on fast growers, so it tends to outrun plain index funds in tech-led rallies and lag when growth falls from favor.
TPZ: Companies that generate and deliver electricity: pipeline and gas network owners, power producers and electric utilities, with energy about three-fifths and utilities about a third. It is a focused bet on the build-out of the power grid, and these businesses tend to pay steady dividends.
TSMY: An options strategy built on one stock, Taiwan Semiconductor, the world's biggest contract chipmaker, selling call options against it to turn its price moves into monthly income. The trade-off is capped gains when the stock jumps, and income that rises and falls with market volatility.
USAI: US and Canadian energy infrastructure companies, all of them: pipeline, storage and gas processing businesses that charge fees to move oil and gas around. It is an income-oriented bet on energy plumbing rather than fuel prices, since these firms earn from volume, not from what a barrel costs.
VABS: Investment-grade bonds backed by pooled loans and property: home mortgages, commercial property loans and asset-backed securities such as auto loan bundles, all actively picked. It aims for steady income with a different flavor of risk than ordinary corporate or government bonds.
XRPI: A single cryptocurrency, XRP, held through linked instruments rather than coins in a wallet, giving brokerage-account access to its price moves. It is a concentrated crypto bet that can swing violently in either direction, with none of the diversification a stock or bond fund provides.
ZDEK: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each December. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZMAR: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each March. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
